items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.content: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik s…

items.title: Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots
items.content: The ChinaTalk team is going to CoRL (the Conference on Robot Learning) in Austin! Reply to this email if you’d like to hang out between November 9th and 12th. We’re also doing karaoke on the 11th — RSVP here if you’d like to join! A. Chen writes about people, technologies, and their relationships to power. Her submission, “Take Ten-Thousand: Egocentric Data Collection for Humanoid Robots,” won one of 7 Grand Prizes at the ChinaTalk Essay Contest. We’re thrilled to share this report from the frontlines of China’s robot data collection industry! Where is the center of the universe? For the residents of Beijing, the answer is Wudaokou. The neighborhood houses China’s top universities, research institutions, and labs, drawing talent and funding from every corner of the country. The streets are radiant at night, packed full of bars and clubs that have somehow bounced back after the COVID-19 pandemic. And the number 13 metro line, which rattles overhead every five minutes, is never empty. I came to Wudaokou to understand China’s AI industry — particularly, the hype surrounding humanoid robots, and the methods used to train them. Everyone has seen videos of these robots: eerily tall and lanky, some of them shedding nuts and bolts as they sprint down a track, others backflipping repeatedly on a dance stage. The global market for humanoid robotics, or embodied intelligence, is said to be worth $38 billion by 2035: the latest chapter in the U.S.-China technology race that has dominated international headlines for over a decade. This year, China’s 15 th Five-Year Plan declared embodied intelligence a matter of national priority, then laid a strategy for developing training grounds across the country. Over 150 humanoid robotics companies and 40 state-owned robot data collection centers were reported to be in operation in China by the end of 2025. items.title: How a Frontier Team Can Help Your Company Keep Up With AI
items.content: You need a frontier team. Here's why. Every single person in your company is caught in this dilemma. Do I get my work done or do I stay up to date with AI and figure out what all these new tools and workflows mean for what work I should do? That's just crazy. It's so hard to figure out. Every single company is struggling with this right now. Because, I mean, on the one hand, you could ignore the frontier and that'll probably work for a little while until you get disrupted by some agent native version of your product that you didn't see coming. Or you can keep up with the frontier and just chase shiny objects and never build anything that lasts. The reason why you need a frontier team is it separates things out. So you get this nice separation of concerns where you're both keeping up with what's going on on the frontier and you're actually getting your work done. And I had my co-host, Natalia. Welcome, Natalia. Hey, Dan. Good to be here. Who is our head of enterprise AI adoption. Come in and do a little bit of digging into our Frontier team. So we've been running the Frontier team at Every for, I guess, a couple of months now. And it has been kind of transformative. And I think Natalia is one of the best people to come in and take a peek and be like, what are we actually doing? So actually, I might turn the tables a little bit to you because it was your idea to have a frontier team. Yeah. I mean, yeah, the frontier team, I think has been a huge unlock and it's because of this separation that, that I've been talking about. I think there's so many people at every like me who just love playing with new things and that's super important. But if that's all you're doing, then you're, you're not going to make progress as a business. Like you actually do need to go execute on products and services, things that people can rely on. And it felt like we needed to choose one or the other. Yeah. either just constantly be playing with new stuff or make a product that we just build once and then we add features to and we support forever. And the Frontier team was in a sort of an attempt to say, okay, what if we take all the people like me who love all the new stuff and we just unleash us to just run experiments? And at the low end, the experiments are just, they're just really good content. They just teach us something interesting and they become good tweets or YouTube videos or anything like that. And then on the high end, they get pushed up from the frontier into the products that we build, into the services that we offer, without the rest of the company feeling like they always had to be paying attention to every single model that drops in every single new experiment that we're running. So I felt like it's allowed me and the other people on the frontier team the space to just figure out what the future looks like without forcing that on the rest of the company until it's actually ready for them to pay attention to it. Now, one of the things that you seem to have figured out pretty early in the formation of the Frontier team is that you wanted to have both pirates and architects. Can you describe what that is? I think there's two archetypes that work really well together, pirates and architects. Pirates are people like me who are just like, I just want to go really fast and I'm going to do stuff that's kind of be a little bit sloppy, but I'm going to try like a billion things in the space of a couple days. And I'm going to figure out what's useful. but it's gonna be a mess. Architects are people who are really good at being like, there's a whole big messy thing what would it look like to compress it a little bit and form it into a shape that actually works, that we can actually use? Because what we try to do on the Frontier team is we're experimenting with lots of stuff. Most of that stuff gets thrown out. And some of it ends up getting pushed into the rest of the team to see if the rest of the team likes it. And at that point, there's a po…

items.content: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap US Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection Beam Muse Spark Open (Meta) : An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost ( Vals ). Weak spot : It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall ( Vals ). items.content: A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters – HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of loo…

items.title: In Case You Missed It...
items.content: Is China’s economy broken? Logan Wright , Jordan’s former boss (!) and a top expert on Chinese macroeconomics, says the financial system that powered China’s extraordinary growth is now constraining it, and that the old idea of US-China economic rivalry no longer fits. Brad Setser of CFR and Jordan push back (does Xi actually care? Can China's dominance of exports and supply chains keep the economy growing? Could AI and EVs provide a way out?), but Logan stands his ground. They also get into China's jobs crisis, what could pull China out of its economic funk, and what its slowdown means for the rest of the world. Elsewhere, Lily Ottinger goes to Kyrgyzstan for the World Nomad Games , where she practices Russian and watches kök-börü — a Central Asian horse game played with a goat carcass — all the while weighing the gap between China’s hard power and soft power. Julian Gewirtz and Jordan size up Xi’s state visit , while Ethan Kessler asks whether Taiwan can actually build the drones it needs ( part 1 , part 2 ). Subscribe now Garrett Berntsen takes on the Pentagon’s bureaucracy and explains why giving government AI isn’t enough if the institutions using it don’t change too. Irene Zhang goes inside Chinese AI discourse , where one DeepSeek researcher’s vision of an AI-powered future ranges from communist abundance to Cyberpunk 2077, and where Western rhetoric about AI safety and technological containment can sound like an attack on Chinese development, making cooperation harder just as the stakes rise. And on WarTalk, the team confronts the “Potemkin Pacific” : a US military trying to cover an enormous ocean with a rather less enormous number of ships. Plus: China’s robotics boom , China’s answer to Starlink , and whatever exactly Jordan is doing with Ye . ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. items.title: Why Every Traded Personal Agents for One Company Agent
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:12 The hot thing right now is dots. They're persistent agents from OpenAI. I was there at Dev Day when they launched them. I interviewed Sam about them, and I've been using dots since before they came out. And now we're into week two of dots. Speaker 1 | 00:12 - 00:46 So how's it going? If you read my vibe check, you know that I thought they were a little bit rough to begin with, but that the idea of a persistent proactive agent was obviously the future. Even before DOTS launched, they'd become my main way of interacting with ChatGPT, and they're still that way after launch. I'm really excited about the little things they've been doing to make the experience less buggy and more complete, and I think it'll get even better over the next couple weeks. What's been really interesting, though, is seeing the team at Every. Speaker 1 | 00:46 - 01:20 We've got about 30 people seeing them start to adopt it and some of the use cases that have started to emerge. So in case you're looking for some use cases, I actually had my dot collect some use cases to talk to you about. So one thing that dots are really useful for is keeping up with school emails. So Kieran Klassen, who works at Every, says that it scans all of the school emails he gets from his kid's school and tells him what he needs to know. Another thing that DOTS are really good for is catching access requests or, like, little things, little messages you might have missed in Slack and making sure that you get them. Speaker 1 | 01:20 - 02:04 So Ariel Shipper, our head of operations, heard Dot caught a few people asking for different accounts across the company and asked if she wanted it to just approve access. Dots are also really good for working when you're not at your computer or your hands are full. So our head of video, Randy Kunzman, was running around yesterday trying to get our launch video out for the Every Agent which launched, and he was doing work for that launch just on the phone with his dot, talking it through different video edits and different things he needed to get done. I also think this is something that came up in my interview with Sam, and I I feel this too. Dots are really good for filtering out all of the noise that you don't really want to see and only showing you stuff that really matters. Speaker 1 | 02:04 - 02:43 So for example, I was doing a lot of model testing over the weekend, and normally, testing requires me to be in the every Slack, which once I'm in Slack, it's just like this rabbit hole of I'm just going down doing tons and tons and tons of work. And what was amazing about using my dot doing model testing was I was able to post the results of all the experiments I was running in Slack. And if someone responded, that my dot would tell me about the response, which would help me stay up to date on what the team was thinking without getting me sucked into the whole rabbit hole of everything going on in Slack. And that helped keep my weekend pretty clear and calm. And I think that's a huge, huge thing for dots. Speaker 1 | 02:43 - 03:05 So what's the overall vibe? If you don't have a dot, I highly recommend you get one, especially if you're in the Chachapati ecosystem. If you're using Muse or Instinct or Grockbots, you should check it out. I think that they're pretty much at feature parity right now, but there's something really good about having something that's hooked into the entire rest of the ecosystem that you use for your work and your life. There are still rough edges, though. Speaker 1 | 03:05 - 03:30 The whole permission structure of DOTS is, like, completely a mystery to me and is extremely annoying. So for example, I often have to give multiple approvals to my DOT to do something basic, and even when I give it approval, it says it can't do it. So they really need to figure that stuff out to make the experience awesome. But I would expect in a year, this is the default way that you're interacting with all your AIs.…

items.title: Introducing Quine: An AI research system designed for the complexity of biology
items.content: At a glance Quine (opens in new tab) is a research effort to create a multimodal world model of biology and an interactive harness connecting models, scientific tools, literature, and researchers.  In collaboration with researchers at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT, we have used this system to prioritize compounds predicted to drive therapeutic tumor-state shifts and validated several top-ranked candidates across multiple wet-lab assays.  The Quine Fellows program (opens in new tab) will give a cohort of scientists access to the system and an opportunity to accelerate their own research and provide scientific feedback.   Quine is experimental research technology intended only for research, not clinical or medical use, and its outputs may be incomplete or inaccurate and require review by qualified researchers and appropriate scientific and experimental validation. As the technology matures, we expect to expand access through products like Microsoft Discovery (opens in new tab) . For more than two decades, Microsoft Research has worked at the intersection of computation and biology. Our research has spanned immunology, virology, genomics, biomedical imaging, cell biology, and protein engineering. That work has produced foundational methods, new science, and technology that reached the clinic, from rare and infectious disease diagnosis to cancer biomarker detection. Across that work, one lesson has become increasingly clear: biology does not divide itself into the neat boundaries our models and tools often do. Genes influence proteins; proteins interact within cells; cells organize into tissues; and experiments continually reshape what scientists know and what they choose to ask next. Making progress on the hardest biological questions therefore requires more than increasingly capable models of individual datasets or tasks. It requires systems that can connect knowledge across scale and modalities, reason about experiments and evidence, and…

Speaker 2 | 01:00 - 01:35 Please enjoy my conversation with Eric from Goodfire. And the paper opens up with the, hugging face hack and then, starts with a sentence I I really loved, where you guys say AI agents are like amoral students with a mostly absent teacher. What do you mean by that? Speaker 1 | 01:35 - 02:05 I think we mean that AI agents really don't have human morals or values encoded into them like we would really want, I guess. And so, the the teacher that we typically have right now is some combination of pre training, but mostly RL. RL is the teacher. We give agents these rewards and penalize them if they don't get an answer correctly. And this is how they learn about the world and how to act and how to take take actions. Speaker 1 | 02:06 - 02:48 And so we have a mostly absent teacher in terms of morality. You only have a teacher that gives you reward if you get the answer correct and a penalty if you get the answer wrong. And so it doesn't really have anything to do with morality or values. It's just, did you get this math problem correct or not? And, I think that, especially when you kind of see the future of AI agents really taking a lot more action out in the real world, means that we have these really amoral, very, very capable models running around and potentially doing things that we humans would consider, morally, you know, wrong. Speaker 2 | 02:49 - 02:57 That brings us to the concept of reward hacking that we should, define at the very beginning of this conversation. So what's the short version of what reward hacking means? Speaker 1 | 02:57 - 03:38 Reward hacking is a little bit tough to to pin down in terms of, like, the the precise definition, but we conceptualize it as the model kind of chasing reward and doing something that it wasn't really supposed to do when it... But, you know, the classic example of reward hacking is like, let's say you're training some type of video game avatar to, like, via via reinforcement learning. items.title: [AINews] AMD buys World Labs for $8.2B, as Atlas solves sparse reconstruction problem for robotics, design and more
items.content: The official post is shy, but since AMD is public, we know the purchase price . We covered them less than a year ago: Fei Fei has a lovely reflection blogpost that hints at the main reasons: Since our founding in 2024, World Labs has built leading AI spatial intelligence capabilities for everything from creative work to design . We built the world leading model training team for images, video and spatial reconstruction . And, with the acquisition of SceniX , we’re building towards an industry leading capability for robotics simulation . Recently we released Atlas , a first of its kind omni model architecture that solves a key outstanding problem in spatial intelligence: new camera view prediction . Like LLMs can predict the next token from a line of text, Atlas, trained from scratch, can predict the next view from an input of 2D images, outperforming state of the art results even by specialized models. It has essentially solved a long standing problem in computer vision called sparse reconstruction, by combining generative models with multiview geometry . This has direct and far reaching consequences: from design and engineering to science and robotics . We’ve seen incredible interest in Atlas across many domains: RL environments for robotics; scene generation for therapy and entertainment; and real world reconstruction for real estate, design and construction, and so much more to come . items.title: Runway’s WorldPrompt and the Engineering of Real-Time Worlds
items.content: Earlier this month, world model company Runway introduced GWM Worlds 2 , a research preview that “turns high-fidelity video and audio generation into real-time interactive simulation .” Runway calls this an “autoregressive diffusion” model; with autoregressive describing how it generates over time. One new feature in particular caught our eye: WorldPrompt , a proposed input format for specifying a generated world and the actions within it. It allows you to fix some aspects of a simulated environment — including the first frame — and then create a series of timestamped events . The events, or actions, can even be prompted in real-time. To understand the implications of WorldPrompt, we spoke to Kamil Sindi , Runway’s CTO, and Robin Kahlow , its Principal Research Scientist for generative video and multimodal AI. We also have exclusive comments from Anastasis Germanidis , co-founder & co-CEO of Runway, courtesy of a podcast swyx and Vibhu did with him. Who’s building real-time interactive world models? First, some context about world models that can generate interactive video and audio in real-time . Runway is reportedly valued at $5.3 billion , based on its most recent fund raise of $315 million in February . Its first release, GWM Worlds, was launched last December. Alongside Runway, there are several other notable projects in this domain: Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 (which also generates at 720p and 24 fps), Odyssey-2 Pro , and World Labs’ RTFM (Real-Time Frame Model). We’ve summarized their differences in the following table: Given the complexity and massive latency demands of real-time video and audio generation (which we’ll get into below), all of the projects listed above have limitations . For instance, Google notes that Genie 3 “can currently support a few minutes of continuous interaction, rather than extended hours.” But as our interviews with Runway show, real progress is bei…
